_metadata.description: Seeded court and administrative rulings relevant to FBA inventory nexus, economic nexus, and franchise tax for ecommerce sellers. These are starting positions as of early 2026 — verify currency before relying on any ruling.
_metadata.disclaimer: This is a research aid, not legal advice. Consult a qualified multi-state tax professional before acting on any ruling.

court_rulings.court: Supreme Court of the United States
court_rulings.holding_summary: Overruled Quill Corp. v. North Dakota, eliminating the physical-presence requirement for sales tax nexus. States may require remote sellers to collect and remit sales tax based on economic activity (economic nexus) without physical presence.
court_rulings.holding_detail: The Court held that the Commerce Clause does not require physical presence for sales tax obligations. South Dakota's economic nexus law ($100,000 in sales or 200 transactions) was upheld as satisfying the Complete Auto test. The Court emphasized the law's safe harbor, non-retroactivity, and South Dakota's SST membership as factors.
court_rulings.relevance_to_fba: Foundational — enabled all states to adopt economic nexus. FBA sellers now face nexus through both physical inventory presence AND economic thresholds. Pre-Wayfair, physical presence (including FBA inventory) was the only nexus theory.
court_rulings.relevance_to_remote_sellers: Every remote seller must now monitor sales volume per state. The ruling did not eliminate physical nexus — it added economic nexus as an independent basis.
court_rulings.status_notes: Landmark precedent. All 45 sales-tax states plus DC have adopted economic nexus laws post-Wayfair.
key_quotes: Physical presence is not necessary to create a substantial nexus.
Each year, the physical presence rule becomes further removed from economic reality.
court_rulings.practical_impact: All remote sellers must track sales by state and register once thresholds are met. The 200-transaction test from SD's law was widely copied but is being phased out by many states.

court_rulings.holding_summary: The court found that the mere presence of inventory in Amazon FBA warehouses in Pennsylvania, without more, was insufficient to establish sales tax nexus or corporate net income tax nexus for the marketplace sellers in the specific facts of the case.
court_rulings.holding_detail: The Online Merchants Guild challenged PA's position that FBA inventory alone created nexus for third-party sellers. The court analyzed the degree of control sellers have over where Amazon places inventory and found the sellers lacked sufficient purposeful direction of activity into PA. The opinion distinguished situations where sellers have more control or direction over inventory placement. Pennsylvania's Department of Revenue had previously taken an aggressive stance that any inventory in PA warehouses created nexus.
court_rulings.relevance_to_fba: CRITICAL — This is the leading case specifically addressing whether FBA inventory alone creates nexus for marketplace sellers. However, the holding is limited: (1) it is a PA Commonwealth Court decision, not binding outside PA; (2) the specific facts involved sellers who did not direct inventory to PA; (3) PA DOR may continue to assert nexus in cases with additional contacts; (4) the ruling's scope regarding the interaction of marketplace facilitator collection with seller filing obligations is still being interpreted.
court_rulings.relevance_to_remote_sellers: Sellers with FBA inventory in PA should be aware that while this ruling provides a basis for arguing no nexus from FBA alone, the PA DOR has not fully conceded the position. Conservative practice still favors registration if inventory is present.
court_rulings.status_notes: Good law in PA as of 2026. Limited to PA Commonwealth Court. PA DOR response and enforcement posture should be monitored. Other states are not bound by this decision but may find its reasoning persuasive. No subsequent appeal resulted in reversal as of the seed date.
key_quotes: The mere storage of inventory in a third-party warehouse, over which the seller exercises no meaningful control regarding location, does not establish the purposeful direction necessary for nexus.
court_rulings.practical_impact: Provides the strongest existing legal argument that FBA inventory alone does not create nexus. However, most tax practitioners still recommend conservative registration because: (1) other states may not follow PA; (2) additional contacts (advertising, returns, etc.) could distinguish the case; (3) the cost of registration may be lower than the risk of back-assessment.

court_rulings.court: Supreme Court of the United States
court_rulings.holding_summary: Required physical presence in a state for sales tax nexus under the Commerce Clause. Overruled by Wayfair in 2018.
court_rulings.holding_detail: Reaffirmed the National Bellas Hess physical presence requirement for sales tax collection. The Court held that the Commerce Clause prohibits states from requiring sales tax collection by sellers without physical presence.
court_rulings.relevance_to_fba: Historical context. Under Quill, FBA inventory in a state DID create physical presence nexus (the inventory was physically there). Wayfair added economic nexus but did not eliminate physical nexus — both theories now coexist.
court_rulings.relevance_to_remote_sellers: Overruled for economic nexus purposes but the physical presence analysis remains relevant for pre-Wayfair periods and for entity-level taxes that may still require physical presence.
court_rulings.status_notes: Overruled by South Dakota v. Wayfair (2018) regarding the physical presence requirement for sales tax nexus.
court_rulings.practical_impact: No longer controlling for sales tax nexus. Historical importance for understanding the evolution of nexus law.

court_rulings.case_name: Braidwood Management v. California Franchise Tax Board (OTA Appeals)
court_rulings.holding_summary: Multiple OTA decisions have addressed whether out-of-state LLCs with FBA inventory in California are 'doing business' in the state and subject to the $800 minimum annual LLC franchise tax. The OTA has generally sustained the FTB's position that inventory storage in CA constitutes doing business.
court_rulings.holding_detail: The California Franchise Tax Board has consistently taken the position that storing inventory in California — including through FBA — constitutes 'doing business' under Revenue & Taxation Code § 23101, triggering the $800 minimum LLC franchise tax regardless of whether the LLC is registered to do business in CA. The OTA has generally upheld this position in multiple appeals, though specific fact patterns vary. The analysis focuses on whether the taxpayer's activities in California, including through agents or third parties, constitute engaging in business.
court_rulings.relevance_to_fba: CRITICAL for CA — FBA sellers with inventory in CA warehouses face a strong risk of the $800 annual LLC franchise tax. This applies even if Amazon handles all sales tax collection as marketplace facilitator. The franchise tax is an entity-level tax separate from sales tax.
court_rulings.relevance_to_remote_sellers: Any LLC selling through FBA should evaluate CA franchise tax exposure if inventory has been or is being stored in CA. The $800 minimum applies from the first day of doing business.
court_rulings.status_notes: OTA decisions are not formally binding as precedent but represent the current enforcement stance. FTB continues to assert this position actively. Monitor for any legislative or superior court changes.
key_quotes: The storage of inventory within this state, even through a third-party arrangement, constitutes an activity that goes beyond the mere solicitation of sales.
court_rulings.practical_impact: FBA sellers with CA inventory should assume $800/year LLC franchise tax liability unless they have a strong factual basis to distinguish their situation. Many practitioners recommend filing the CA LLC return and paying the $800 as the cost-effective compliance approach rather than risking penalties and interest on assessment.

court_rulings.case_name: Tyler Pipe Industries, Inc. v. Washington State Dept. of Revenue
court_rulings.court: Supreme Court of the United States
court_rulings.holding_summary: Established that the activities of an in-state agent or representative can establish nexus for an out-of-state seller, even if the seller has no direct physical presence. The presence of property (including inventory held by others) can contribute to nexus analysis.
court_rulings.holding_detail: The Court held that the presence of sales representatives in Washington who were independent contractors created sufficient nexus for B&O tax. The decision established that nexus can arise from the activities of in-state agents and is part of the foundation for the argument that third-party warehousing (including FBA) creates nexus.
court_rulings.relevance_to_fba: Tyler Pipe's agent-nexus theory is one basis states use to argue that FBA inventory creates nexus — Amazon acts as an agent storing the seller's property. The Online Merchants Guild case in PA pushes back on this theory for FBA specifically.
court_rulings.relevance_to_remote_sellers: Remains relevant for B&O and other business activity taxes in Washington and for the general principle that in-state property or agents create nexus.
court_rulings.status_notes: Good law. Physical-presence nexus analysis from Tyler Pipe coexists with Wayfair's economic nexus. Tyler Pipe is key to understanding why most states treat FBA inventory as nexus-creating.
court_rulings.practical_impact: Supports the majority position that FBA inventory creates physical nexus via the agent/property theory.

admin_rulings.title: Oklahoma Tax Commission — Third-Party Fulfillment Inventory Position
admin_rulings.summary: Oklahoma has issued guidance suggesting that inventory stored in a third-party fulfillment center (including FBA) where the seller does not control the location of inventory placement may not, by itself, create sufficient nexus for sales tax purposes, particularly in the context of marketplace facilitator collection.
admin_rulings.detail: The OTC's position is nuanced: while property in the state generally creates nexus, the interaction with marketplace facilitator laws means that even if nexus exists, the marketplace facilitator (Amazon) is responsible for collection. The practical impact on the seller's own filing obligations is reduced. However, the seller may still need to register and file zero returns. The OTC has not issued a formal published ruling definitively stating FBA alone does not create nexus.
admin_rulings.relevance_to_fba: Oklahoma is among the states that take a more measured approach to FBA inventory nexus, partly due to marketplace facilitator collection covering the tax obligation.
admin_rulings.relevance_to_remote_sellers: Sellers with FBA inventory in OK should still evaluate registration, but the practical filing burden is lower due to marketplace facilitator collection. Monitor for formal guidance.
admin_rulings.status_notes: Informal guidance. No formal published ruling. Position could change.
admin_rulings.practical_impact: Low practical risk for sellers relying on Amazon as marketplace facilitator for OK sales. Registration may still be technically required.

admin_rulings.title: Texas Comptroller — Remote Seller and Marketplace Guidance
admin_rulings.summary: Texas Comptroller's Rule 3.286 and related guidance establish that remote sellers with inventory stored in Texas (including through FBA) have physical nexus. The $500,000 economic nexus threshold applies separately. Texas also requires franchise tax filing for entities doing business in the state.
admin_rulings.detail: Texas takes an aggressive position on FBA inventory nexus. The Comptroller has publicly stated that inventory stored in Texas warehouses creates nexus for both sales tax and franchise tax purposes. The franchise tax has a ~$2.47M total revenue exemption (no tax owed below this), but the No Tax Due report and Public Information Report must still be filed annually by May 15. Failure to file can result in forfeiture of the right to do business in Texas.
admin_rulings.relevance_to_fba: Texas is a major FBA warehouse state with multiple fulfillment centers. Sellers almost certainly have inventory there. Both sales tax nexus and franchise tax filing obligations are triggered.
admin_rulings.relevance_to_remote_sellers: Even if Amazon collects and remits sales tax as marketplace facilitator, the seller may need to register and file. The franchise tax filing obligation is independent of sales tax.
admin_rulings.practical_impact: FBA sellers must evaluate both sales tax and franchise tax obligations in TX. The franchise tax filing is often overlooked and carries real penalties for non-filing.

admin_rulings.title: California CDTFA — Registration Requirements for Remote Sellers and Marketplace Sellers
admin_rulings.issuing_agency: California Department of Tax and Fee Administration
admin_rulings.summary: CDTFA guidance on when remote sellers and marketplace sellers must register for a CA seller's permit. Inventory stored in CA creates nexus. Economic nexus threshold is $500,000 in sales (including marketplace sales). The $800 LLC franchise tax (FTB, not CDTFA) is a separate obligation.
admin_rulings.detail: California has a higher economic nexus threshold ($500,000 vs. the common $100,000) but includes marketplace sales in the calculation. For FBA sellers, physical nexus from inventory is the more common trigger. CDTFA has been active in identifying and contacting FBA sellers with CA inventory. The franchise tax board (FTB) separately pursues the $800 LLC franchise tax.
admin_rulings.relevance_to_fba: Both sales tax (CDTFA) and franchise tax (FTB) obligations arise from FBA inventory in CA. These are enforced by separate agencies.
admin_rulings.relevance_to_remote_sellers: CA's $500,000 economic threshold is higher than most states, but marketplace sales count. Physical presence from FBA inventory is often the nexus trigger for smaller sellers.
admin_rulings.practical_impact: FBA sellers must address both CDTFA (sales tax) and FTB (franchise tax) obligations. Two separate registrations and filing regimes.

admin_rulings.title: Streamlined Sales Tax Governing Board — Taxability Matrix: General Rules
admin_rulings.summary: The SST Taxability Matrix provides state-by-state product taxability information for SST member states. Tangible personal property (including skincare/cosmetic products) is generally taxable in all SST member states unless specifically exempt.
admin_rulings.detail: The SST matrices cover product taxability, not nexus. They confirm that most tangible personal property (including tallow-based skincare products) is taxable. Some states exempt certain health/medical items, but cosmetic and skincare products are almost universally taxable. The matrices are useful for confirming product taxability assumptions and for identifying any state-specific exemptions.
admin_rulings.relevance_to_fba: Confirms product taxability assumptions. Tallow-based skincare is taxable tangible personal property in all states with sales tax.
admin_rulings.practical_impact: Supports the system's assumption that all products are fully taxable. Review if product line expands to items that might qualify for exemptions.

admin_rulings.title: Washington DOR — FBA Sellers and B&O Tax Guidance
admin_rulings.summary: Washington DOR guidance addressing FBA sellers' B&O tax obligations. Washington's B&O tax applies to gross receipts from business conducted in Washington. FBA inventory in WA warehouses constitutes doing business in WA. Washington also includes marketplace sales in the $100,000 economic nexus threshold calculation.
admin_rulings.detail: Washington is notable for having both a sales tax and a separate B&O (Business & Occupation) tax. The B&O tax applies to the seller's gross receipts, not just retail sales tax. FBA sellers with WA inventory may owe B&O tax on their Washington-sourced income in addition to any sales tax obligations. The marketplace facilitator handles sales tax collection, but B&O tax is the seller's own obligation. Multiple B&O classifications exist; retailing is the most common for ecommerce sellers.
admin_rulings.relevance_to_fba: WA B&O tax is a separate obligation from sales tax and is not covered by marketplace facilitator collection. FBA inventory creates the nexus for B&O purposes.
admin_rulings.relevance_to_remote_sellers: B&O tax is frequently overlooked by remote sellers focused only on sales tax. The rates are relatively low (0.471% retailing) but apply to gross receipts, not net income.
admin_rulings.practical_impact: FBA sellers with WA inventory should evaluate B&O tax obligations separately from sales tax. This is a separate registration and filing requirement.
